subject: Chemistry
title: Organic Chemistry
learningOutcomes: Define and draw displayed and condensed (normal) structural formulae, and use the rule that every carbon atom forms four bonds.
Name and draw unbranched alkanes, and build any organic name from a stem plus a suffix.
Name and draw unbranched alkenes, including but-1-ene and but-2-ene, and apply the numbering rule.
Name and draw unbranched alkynes, including but-1-yne and but-2-yne.
Name and draw unbranched alcohols, including propan-1-ol, propan-2-ol, butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol.
Name and draw unbranched carboxylic acids and explain why no number is needed for the –COOH group.
State the type of a compound from its name ending (-ane, -ene, -yne, -ol, -oic acid, -oate) or from its molecular, condensed or displayed formula.
Name and draw unbranched esters made from alcohols and carboxylic acids of up to four carbon atoms, and explain esterification.

sections.heading: Organic Chemistry and the Four-Bond Rule
sections.body: Organic chemistry is the study of carbon-based compounds, which are found in living things, fuels, medicines, plastics, foods and perfumes. A hydrocarbon contains carbon and hydrogen only. A functional group is an atom or group of atoms that decides the class of an organic compound. In organic compounds every carbon atom forms four bonds, every hydrogen atom forms one bond and every oxygen atom forms two bonds. Because carbon forms four bonds, carbon atoms can join into chains and make a huge number of different compounds.

sections.heading: Structural Formulae: Displayed and Condensed
sections.body: A structural formula shows how the atoms in a molecule are joined up. A displayed formula shows every atom and every bond as a separate line: a single bond is one line, a double bond is two lines and a triple bond is three lines. It shows clearly how atoms are connected but is very large and time-consuming to draw. A condensed (normal) formula groups the atoms joined to the same carbon and drops the bonds, for example CH₃CH₃ for ethane and CH₃CH₂CH₃ for propane. The group –CH₃ is called the methyl group and –CH₂– is called the methylene group. A molecular formula such as C₃H₈ only counts the atoms.

sections.heading: Alkanes
sections.body: Alkanes are hydrocarbons in which all the carbon atoms are joined by single covalent bonds. Their general formula is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. In an unbranched alkane each end carbon carries three hydrogen atoms and each middle carbon carries two. The first members are methane CH₄, ethane CH₃CH₃, propane CH₃CH₂CH₃, butane CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ and pentane CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃. A long chain can be written in a shorter way, for example CH₃(CH₂)₃CH₃ for pentane.

sections.heading: Alkenes
sections.body: Alkenes are hydrocarbons with at least one carbon–carbon double bond (C=C). Their general formula is CₙH₂ₙ. A double bond is formed when two carbon atoms share two pairs of electrons and is drawn as two lines. A doubly bonded carbon atom forms single bonds with two other atoms. The simplest alkene is ethene CH₂=CH₂, followed by propene CH₃CH=CH₂. Butene exists as but-1-ene CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ and but-2-ene CH₃CH=CHCH₃; they have the same molecular formula C₄H₈ but different structures.

sections.heading: Alkynes
sections.body: Alkynes are hydrocarbons with at least one carbon–carbon triple bond (C≡C). The general formula of alkynes with one triple bond is CₙH₂ₙ₋₂. A triple bond is formed when two carbon atoms share three pairs of electrons and is drawn as three lines. The simplest alkyne is ethyne CH≡CH, also called acetylene; each carbon in ethyne is bonded to one hydrogen atom. Next come propyne CH₃C≡CH, but-1-yne CH≡CCH₂CH₃ and but-2-yne CH₃C≡CCH₃; the two butynes both have the molecular formula C₄H₆.

sections.heading: The IUPAC Naming System
sections.body: IUPAC stands for the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry. It gives standard rules for naming compounds from their structure, so chemists everywhere can identify them and avoid the confusion of common names. Every IUPAC name is built from a stem and a suffix. The stem tells the number of carbon atoms in the longest chain: meth 1, eth 2, prop 3, but 4, pent 5, hex 6, hept 7, oct 8, non 9, dec 10. The suffix tells the family: -ane alkane, -ene alkene, -yne alkyne, -ol alcohol, -oic acid carboxylic acid, and alkyl … -oate for an ester. The letters a, e, y in -ane, -ene, -yne match 1, 2, 3 bonds (single, double, triple).

sections.heading: The Numbering Rule
sections.body: In longer chains a number in the name shows where the double bond, the triple bond or the –OH group is. The chain is numbered from the end that gives the smaller number. For example CH₃CH₂CH=CHCH₃ is pent-2-ene, not pent-3-ene. In but-1-ene the double bond is between C-1 and C-2, and in but-2-ene it is between C-2 and C-3. Ethene, propene, ethyne and propyne need no number.

sections.heading: Alcohols
sections.body: Alcohols contain the hydroxyl group –OH attached to a carbon chain (R–OH). To name an alcohol, replace the final “e” of the alkane name by “ol”: methanol CH₃OH and ethanol CH₃CH₂OH. From three carbons upward a number shows the carbon that carries the –OH group: propan-1-ol CH₃CH₂CH₂OH and propan-2-ol CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ both have the molecular formula C₃H₈O. In the same way there are butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol. A –OH on a middle carbon is written in brackets in the condensed formula. In –OH the oxygen lies between carbon and hydrogen (C–O–H), and the –OH is covalently bonded, so it does not make the compound an alkali.

sections.heading: Carboxylic Acids
sections.body: Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl group –COOH, a carbon that carries both a double-bonded oxygen (C=O) and an –OH group. The general formula is RCOOH. To name them, replace the final “e” of the alkane name by “oic acid”: methanoic acid HCOOH (formic acid), ethanoic acid CH₃COOH (acetic acid), propanoic acid CH₃CH₂COOH (propionic acid), butanoic acid and pentanoic acid. No number is written because the –COOH carbon is always carbon 1. Their molecular formulae are CH₂O₂, C₂H₄O₂, C₃H₆O₂ and C₄H₈O₂ for the first four.

sections.heading: Esters and Esterification
sections.body: Esters are compounds derived from carboxylic acids and alcohols; they have the group –COO– between two carbon groups, the general formula RCOOR′ and a fruity smell. Esterification is the reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol to form an ester and water, using a few drops of sulphuric acid as catalyst and heating: RCOOH + R′OH → RCOOR′ + H₂O. The acid gives –OH and the alcohol gives H, and these leave as water. To name an ester, write the alkyl group from the alcohol first and the acid part second, changing “-ic acid” to “-ate”: ethanoic acid + methanol → methyl ethanoate. Sixteen unbranched esters can be made from the C1–C4 alcohols and C1–C4 acids.

sections.heading: Identifying the Type of a Compound
sections.body: The name ending tells the family: -ane alkane, -ene alkene, -yne alkyne, -ol alcohol, -oic acid carboxylic acid, alkyl … -oate ester. From a formula, first check which elements are present. If there is only carbon and hydrogen, look for a C≡C bond (alkyne); if none, look for a C=C bond (alkene); if none, it is an alkane. If oxygen is present, look for –COOH (carboxylic acid); if none, look for –COO– between two carbon groups (ester); if none, look for –OH on a carbon chain (alcohol). Compounds with the same molecular formula can belong to different families, for example C₃H₆O₂ is propanoic acid, methyl ethanoate or ethyl methanoate.

definitions.definition: The study of carbon-based compounds.
A compound that contains carbon and hydrogen only.
An atom or group of atoms that decides the class of an organic compound.
A formula that shows how the different atoms are joined up or arranged in a molecule.
A structural formula that shows every atom and every bond as an individual line.
A structural formula that omits some or all bonds and groups the atoms joined to the same carbon, e.g. CH₃CH₂CH₃.
The –CH₃ group.
The –CH₂– group.
Hydrocarbons in which all the carbon atoms are joined by single covalent bonds; general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
Hydrocarbons with at least one carbon–carbon double bond; general formula CₙH₂ₙ.
Hydrocarbons with at least one carbon–carbon triple bond; general formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ for one triple bond.
International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry, which gives the standard rules for naming organic compounds.
The part of an IUPAC name that tells the number of carbon atoms in the longest chain (meth, eth, prop, but …).
The ending of an IUPAC name that tells the family of the compound (-ane, -ene, -yne, -ol, -oic acid, -oate).
Organic compounds that contain the hydroxyl group –OH attached to a carbon chain.
The –OH functional group of alcohols.
Organic compounds that contain the carboxyl group –COOH; general formula RCOOH.
The –COOH functional group: a carbon with a double-bonded oxygen (C=O) and an –OH group.
Organic compounds derived from carboxylic acids and alcohols, with the group –COO– between two carbon groups; general formula RCOOR′.
The reaction between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol to form an ester and water, in the presence of a few drops of sulphuric acid as catalyst.

examTips: Learn the stems 1–4 as “Mice Eat Peanut Butter” = meth, eth, prop, but; stems 5–10 match pentagon, hexagon, heptagon, octagon, nonagon, decagon.
The letters a – e – y in -ane, -ene, -yne match 1 – 2 – 3 bonds: single, double and triple.
Always count four bonds on every carbon atom after drawing a formula; if a carbon has three or five bonds, the drawing is wrong.
Numbering rule: number the chain from the end that gives the smaller number to the double bond, triple bond or –OH group. CH₃CH₂CH=CHCH₃ is pent-2-ene, not pent-3-ene.
No number is needed for ethene, propene, ethyne, propyne or for carboxylic acids, because the –COOH carbon is always carbon 1.
Name an alcohol by replacing the final “e” of the alkane by “ol”, and a carboxylic acid by replacing it with “oic acid”.
An ester name has two words: the alkyl part from the alcohol comes first, the acid part (-ic acid → -ate) comes second. CH₃COOCH₃ is methyl ethanoate, not “ethanoate methyl”.
Esterification: carboxylic acid + alcohol → ester + water, with a few drops of sulphuric acid as catalyst and heating. The acid gives –OH, the alcohol gives H.
Drawing recipe (name → formula): stem gives the carbons, suffix gives the family, place the double bond / triple bond / –OH / –COOH, then add hydrogens until every carbon has four bonds.
Learn the common names of the first acids: methanoic acid = formic acid, ethanoic acid = acetic acid, propanoic acid = propionic acid; ethyne is also called acetylene.
To identify a compound from its formula: only C and H → look for C≡C, then C=C, else alkane. With oxygen → –COOH (acid), then –COO– (ester), then –OH (alcohol).
Different compounds can share one molecular formula (C₃H₆O₂ = propanoic acid, methyl ethanoate, ethyl methanoate), so always check the functional group, not just the formula.

practiceQuestions.prompt: How many bonds does every carbon atom form in an organic compound?
practiceQuestions.explanation: In organic compounds each carbon atom forms four bonds, each hydrogen forms one and each oxygen forms two.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which name ending shows that a compound is an alkene?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The endings -ane, -ene and -yne show single, double and triple bonds (a – e – y = 1 – 2 – 3).

practiceQuestions.prompt: What is the name of the alkane with three carbon atoms?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The stem prop means three carbon atoms and -ane shows an alkane, so the name is propane, CH₃CH₂CH₃.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which functional group is present in a carboxylic acid?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl group –COOH, a carbon with a C=O and an –OH on the same atom.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What is the condensed structural formula of propene?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Propene has three carbons and one C=C double bond, so its condensed formula is CH₃CH=CH₂ (C₃H₆).
The 2 in propan-2-ol shows that –OH is on the middle carbon, which is written in brackets: CH₃CH(OH)CH₃.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What is the correct name of CH₃CH₂CH=CHCH₃?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Numbering from the right gives the double bond the smaller number (2), so the name is pent-2-ene, not pent-3-ene.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which pair of compounds reacts, with a few drops of sulphuric acid, to form methyl ethanoate?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The first word “methyl” comes from methanol and “ethanoate” comes from ethanoic acid: CH₃COOH + CH₃OH → CH₃COOCH₃ + H₂O.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Alkenes have at least one carbon–carbon double bond.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Alkenes are hydrocarbons with at least one C=C double bond; their general formula is CₙH₂ₙ.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The ending -yne shows a carbon–carbon double bond.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. The ending -yne shows a C≡C triple bond; the ending -ene shows a C=C double bond.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Esterification produces an ester and water.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Carboxylic acid + alcohol → ester + water, with a few drops of sulphuric acid as catalyst.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A carbon chain is always numbered from its left-hand end.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. The chain is numbered from the end that gives the smaller number to the double bond, triple bond or –OH group.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Compounds that contain only carbon and hydrogen are called ____.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A hydrocarbon is a compound that contains carbon and hydrogen only.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The stem for five carbon atoms is ____.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Pent comes from pentagon (5 sides), so pent means five carbon atoms.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The –COOH group is called the ____ group.
practiceQuestions.explanation: –COOH is the carboxyl group, the functional group of carboxylic acids.

sequencingActivity.prompt: Arrange the steps for drawing the structure of pentane in the correct order.

items: Add hydrogens so every carbon has four bonds
Write a chain of five carbon atoms: C–C–C–C–C
Read the stem “pent” as five carbon atoms
Read the ending “-ane” as an alkane (all single bonds)
correctOrder: Read the stem “pent” as five carbon atoms
Read the ending “-ane” as an alkane (all single bonds)
Write a chain of five carbon atoms: C–C–C–C–C
Add hydrogens so every carbon has four bonds

sequencingActivity.explanation: Read the stem (number of carbons) and the ending (family), write the carbon chain, add hydrogens until each carbon has four bonds, then write the condensed formula.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A compound has the condensed formula CH₃COOCH₃. Which name and family are correct?
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: CH₃COOCH₃ has the –COO– group between two carbon groups, so it is an ester. The CH₃ on the O comes from methanol (methyl) and the CH₃CO– side comes from ethanoic acid (ethanoate).

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Why is CH₃CH₂CH=CHCH₃ named pent-2-ene and NOT pent-3-ene?

options: The chain must always be numbered from the left-hand end
The chain is numbered from the end that gives the double bond the smaller number
The stem “pent” changes when the double bond moves
A double bond is always counted from the carbon with most hydrogens

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Numbering from the right makes the double bond start on carbon 2, which is smaller than 3, so the name is pent-2-ene.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: How are propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol related?

options: The same compound written in two ways
Different compounds with different molecular formulae
Different compounds with the same molecular formula, C₃H₈O
One is an alcohol and the other is an ester

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Both have three carbons and one –OH group (C₃H₈O) but the –OH is on carbon 1 in one and on carbon 2 in the other, so they are different compounds.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Ethanoic acid is heated with ethanol and a few drops of sulphuric acid. Which ester forms and what is its molecular formula?
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: CH₃COOH + CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ + H₂O. The ester is ethyl ethanoate, C₄H₈O₂ (2 + 2 carbons, formula CₙH₂ₙO₂ with n = 4).

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A compound contains only carbon and hydrogen, has no C=C or C≡C bond and has the molecular formula C₆H₁₄. What is the correct conclusion?

options: It is an alkane, hexane (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = 6)

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Only C and H with no multiple bond means an alkane. C₆H₁₄ fits CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = 6, so it is hexane.
